question: What is another name for a hospital-acquired infection?
explanation: Infections caught while receiving medical care in a hospital or clinic are formally called nosocomial infections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is breaking any single link in the chain of infection effective?

options.A: It boosts the patient's natural red blood cell count
options.B: It stops the infectious cycle from continuing
options.C: It permanently destroys all bacteria in the room
options.D: It cures the underlying primary disease immediately

explanation: Because the chain relies on every link connecting, removing or blocking just one link halts the spread of germs. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h1)

question: How many times can a single sterile syringe and needle be used safely?

options.A: For multiple injections on the same patient
options.B: As many times as needed until the needle bends
options.C: For up to three patients if wiped with alcohol
options.D: For exactly one injection on one patient

explanation: Syringes and needles are single-use medical devices meant for one patient and one procedure only. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h2)

question: A nurse finishes drawing up an emergency medication from a single-dose vial. What should be done with the remaining liquid in the vial?

options.A: Save it in the pocket for the next patient
options.B: Put it back into the main supply drawer
options.D: Leave the syringe attached for later use

explanation: Single-dose vials do not contain preservatives, so any leftover medication must be thrown away to prevent microbial growth. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is considered the single most important measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections?
explanation: Cleaning hands correctly removes transient microorganisms acquired from patients and environmental surfaces. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h3)

question: When is it strictly necessary for a nurse to use soap and water instead of an alcohol hand rub?

options.A: Only when starting a surgical procedure in the theater
options.B: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.C: Whenever the alcohol dispenser is empty for the day
options.D: Every time a nurse enters a new hospital ward

explanation: Alcohol rubs cannot remove physical dirt or certain tough bacterial spores as effectively as physical washing with soap and water. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h3)

question: What must a nurse do immediately after wiping a medication vial rubber top with an alcohol swab?

options.A: Allow the alcohol to dry completely before piercing
options.B: Blow on the rubber top to dry it fast
options.C: Insert the needle immediately while it is wet
options.D: Rinse the top with sterile tap water

explanation: Giving the alcohol time to air dry ensures proper disinfection of the rubber stopper surface. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h4)

question: Which part of a sterile syringe must a nurse avoid touching to maintain proper aseptic technique?

options.A: The inner barrel and the plunger shaft
options.B: The outer colored flange of the syringe
options.C: The paper packaging before it is opened
options.D: The outside plastic wall of the barrel

explanation: Touching parts of the syringe that will contact medication or enter the sterile pathway introduces germs directly into the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h4)

question: At what fill level should a clinical sharps container be securely closed and replaced?

options.A: Whenever a new nurse starts a shift
options.B: Only at the end of every working week
options.D: When it is completely packed to the top brim

explanation: Stopping at the three-quarters mark prevents accidental pokes from overflowing needles when dropping items in. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why is two-handed needle recapping strongly discouraged in clinical practice?

options.A: It dramatically increases the risk of an accidental finger puncture
options.B: It makes the plastic syringe barrel crack under pressure
options.C: It violates basic hospital waste management laws for paper
options.D: It causes the medication inside the needle to evaporate

explanation: Holding the cap with one hand and guiding the sharp needle toward it with the other hand frequently leads to missed caps and deep finger injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h5)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take after sustaining an accidental needle-stick injury?

options.A: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water
options.B: Fill out an incident report form for the manager
options.C: Squeeze the finger tightly to push out old blood
options.D: Apply an antiseptic iodine ointment and a bandage

explanation: Immediate washing reduces the viral or bacterial load introduced at the puncture site before it enters the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid aggressively squeezing a needle-stick wound?

options.A: It causes permanent paralysis of the affected finger
options.B: It neutralizes the effect of any washing soap used
options.C: It damages local tissue and can increase pathogen entry
options.D: It makes the bleeding stop too fast for testing

explanation: Squeezing or milking the puncture site tears delicate capillaries, creating a larger pathway for infectious agents to enter circulation. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is a common patient misconception regarding injections that nurses should actively address?

options.A: Expecting nurses to reuse needles to save money for the clinic
options.B: Assuming all vaccines contain active live viruses that cause severe disease
options.C: Thinking that single-use syringes can be washed at home with hot water
options.D: Believing injections are always superior or faster than oral drugs for any illness

explanation: Many patients demand injections unnecessarily, unaware that safe oral medications are often just as effective and carry fewer risks. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h7)

question: A patient asks a student nurse why a new sterile syringe is being opened for every single dose. How should the student best respond?

options.A: Because hospital policy says old plastic gets too brittle to use
options.B: So that the pharmaceutical companies can sell more plastic items
options.C: To make the medication taste better when it enters the body
options.D: To prevent passing infections and germs between different patients

explanation: Explaining that sterile single-use devices stop the transfer of bloodborne germs reassures the patient and reinforces safety standards. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h7)
